Sorcerer
SOR-ser-er
noun
From Old French sorcier, through Late Latin sortiarius, “one who tells fortunes by lots,” from Latin sors, sortis, “lot, fate.” In the New Testament it renders the Greek magos and the pharmakeia word-group, which binds magic to drugs and spells.

Biblical Definition

A sorcerer is a worker of magic arts — one who claims to bend spirits, fate, or nature by spell, drug, and incantation. The English word climbs down from the Latin sors, “a lot” or “fate,” through the sortiarius who told fortunes by casting lots; but Scripture strips the trade of its pretended mastery and shows it always broken before the living God. On Cyprus Paul meets “a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus” (Act 13:6), and when this “Elymas the sorcerer… withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith” (Act 13:8), the apostle strikes him blind for a season — the arts that dazzled the deputy could not keep their own master from groping for a hand to lead him. In Egypt Pharaoh “called the wise men and the sorcerers” (Exo 7:11), and they aped the rod-turned-serpent, only to have Aaron’s rod swallow theirs — a counterfeit permitted just far enough to be humbled. Jeremiah lists sorcerers among the lying voices that promised Judah escape from Babylon (Jer 27:9), and the LORD promises to be “a swift witness against the sorcerers” (Mal 3:5). The demonic power behind the art is not denied; it is dethroned. Sorcery is real rebellion, and Revelation shuts the sorcerer outside the city with the idolaters and the liars.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who practices magic arts by spells, drugs, and incantation, claiming power over spirits or fate.

SORCERER, a person who practices sorcery; a conjurer, an enchanter, a magician.

From Old French sorcier, through Late Latin sortiarius, a teller of fortunes by lots, from sors, “lot, fate.”

In the New Testament it renders the Greek magos and the pharmakeia word-group, joining magic to drugs and spells.

Elymas the sorcerer withstood Paul and was struck blind (Act 13:8); Pharaoh’s sorcerers aped Moses and failed (Exo 7:11).

The LORD promises to be a swift witness against the sorcerers in the day of judgment (Mal 3:5).

Key Scripture

Act 13:6 — "And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus:"

Act 13:8 — "But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith."

Jer 27:9 — "Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon:"

Exo 7:11 — "Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments."

Modern Corruption

Sorcery has revived openly — the “magick” and spell-craft of the neo-pagan movement, and the ritual drug-craft that seeks “spirit journeys” — and it is the same rebellion the apostles confronted.

expand to see more

This is no dead word. A generation raised on wizarding fantasy has taken up literal spell-craft: the bookshop “magick” shelf, the online covens, the ritual candle and sigil sold beside the incense, the “manifesting” that is old sympathetic magic under a self-help name. The Greek behind “sorcerer” is pharmakeia — the union of drug and spell — and the modern drug-craft that hunts visions and “spirit journeys” through hallucinogens is that very thing. The world calls it self-discovery and empowerment; the Word ranks its kindred among the works of the flesh — “idolatry, witchcraft” (Gal 5:20) — that shut men out of the kingdom of God.

The apostolic answer was not debate but repentance and a bonfire. At Ephesus “many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19), counting the price at fifty thousand pieces of silver — the converted sorcerer does not curate his old power, he destroys it. The demonic reality is not to be trifled with, but neither is it to be feared, for the Spirit who dwells in the believer is greater than the spirit at work in the world. Christ spoiled principalities and powers openly, and every sorcerer who bows to Him is snatched from the strong man’s house. The city has an outside, and Revelation leaves the impenitent sorcerer there (Rev 22:15) — but the door stands open now to all who will burn the books and believe.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word traces to sors, “lot, fate” — a fortune-caster and magic-worker; in the New Testament the pharmakeia of drug and spell.

expand to see more

Sorcerer — Old French sorcier, from Latin sors, “lot, fate.”

In the Greek New Testament it renders magos and the pharmakeia word-group.

Elymas the sorcerer was struck blind for withstanding the gospel (Act 13:8).

Pharaoh’s sorcerers imitated Moses with their enchantments, then failed (Exo 7:11).

The LORD will be a swift witness against the sorcerers (Mal 3:5); they are shut out of the city (Rev 22:15).

Usage

"The AV sorcerer is no stage-magician but a real worker of dark arts — Elymas, struck blind before the deputy."

"The Greek word is pharmakeia: drug and spell together, the ancient root of much that is called “magick” today."

"Pharaoh’s sorcerers matched Moses trick for trick — until Aaron’s rod swallowed theirs."
